entry.title: DaVinci Resolve 21.2 Released – PROLED XDR Touch Support, Gen 6 Color Science LUTs, Up to 5x Faster Rendering on M5 Pro and M5 Max
entry.summary: Blackmagic Design has released DaVinci Resolve 21.2, and the headline item is support for Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screen. The update also adds support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks, and Blackmagic claims up to 5x faster render
entry.content:
Blackmagic Design has released DaVinci Resolve 21.2, and the headline item is support for Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screen. The update also adds support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks, and Blackmagic claims up to 5x faster rendering on M5 Pro and M5 Max machines. Editors get multicam clips in source timelines, a shortcut to restore the last active edit points and source timecode for extracted audio, and Studio users get new AI assistant functions.

DaVinci Resolve 21.2, DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 and Fusion Studio 21.2 are available now as free updates for macOS, Windows, Windows for Arm and Linux. Blackmagic published the release notes on November 4, 2026. In both editions, the update adds support for the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, support for Blackmagic Gen 6 LUTs, multicam clips that open as source clips in source timelines, compound clip changes, EXIF metadata in PNG files and a long list of fixes for audio, AAF, OGraf, H.265 and XDCAM media. The Studio version adds ResolveFX False Color support for Gen 5 and Gen 6 color science, new AI assistant functions and “multiple scripting API improvements”. System requirements do not change.

Version 21.2 follows 21.1.2 from late October, which made OGraf playback faster, refined edit point selection on the Edit page and added faster IntelliSearch analysis on M6 Macs in Studio. The larger feature release was DaVinci Resolve 21.1in September, with the native MCP server for AI assistants and individual HDR trims. For the full picture of version 21, read our coverage of the final Resolve 21 release and our hands-on with the Photo page and IntelliSearch at NAB 2026.

Touch and the M5 Pro and M5 Max

Apple announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display on October 28. It is the first Mac with a touch screen, and it uses a tandem OLED panel with 2000 nits peak HDR brightness. At the launch, Apple listed DaVinci Resolve among the third-party apps that would get Touch support later this year, but it did not say what the Resolve implementation would include. Resolve 21.2 now lists “Support for Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screens.” The release notes do not say which pages or controls react to touch, or whether Resolve goes beyond the standard macOS behavior that translates touches into clicks.

The PROLED XDR models use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that Apple introduced in March. In the download description for 21.2, Blackmagic claims “up to 5x faster rendering for M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon chips”. Blackmagic does not say which render formats or which earlier version it compares against, so this is a manufacturer figure without a stated baseline. The item also does not appear in the readme itself, only in the summary on the support page.

Generation 6 color science

Both editions add support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks. Blackmagic introduced Gen 6 color science to its software in September with Blackmagic RAW 6.0, and Resolve 21.2 now accepts the matching LUTs and film looks. In Studio, the ResolveFX False Color tool now also supports Gen 5 and Gen 6 color science, so exposure checks with false color work with the current Blackmagic camera color pipelines.

Editing: multicam, edit points and compound clips

Most of the editorial changes affect source timelines and edit points. Multicam clips now open as source clips in source timelines, and “Open in Timeline with Source Viewer” now supports both clips and multicams. A new menu action and keyboard shortcut restores the last active edit points, and a Command or Ctrl marquee selection now uses the last edit point type. This continues the trim and edit point work of 21.1, 21.1.1 and 21.1.2.

Compound clips get two changes. When you convert an in-out range to a compound clip, Resolve now replaces the clips in place in the timeline. A separate context action creates a compound clip from the in-out range without that replacement. The update also lets you conform lock multiple timeline clips to one media pool clip in one step.

Several smaller changes remove friction in daily work. The “stop playback” option now also applies to playhead nudges and mouse clicks, Edit menu options stay in place after a UI layout reset, and PNG files now carry their EXIF metadata into Resolve.

Audio and interchange fixes

For sound editors, extracted audio files now keep the source timecode. Blackmagic has also improved the decoding speed of MXF audio from network storage, fixed slow renders of MP3 audio-only files and corrected the channel order of WAV files with iXML tracks. An audio input device preference no longer resets after a restart, and pasted clip EQ Q and frequency values are now correct.

On the interchange side, 21.2 fixes missing clips in some AAF imports and wrong audio timecode in AAF files with interlaced media. Imported TTML subtitles now show italics correctly. For collaboration projects, source track changes in source timelines now work as intended.

AI assistants and scripting in Studio

The native MCP server that arrived in Resolve Studio 21.1 lets AI assistants such as Claude control a project with normal language. In 21.2, Blackmagic lists “improved AI assistant color and Fusion capabilities”. AI assistants can now download the extras that some advanced features need, and they can export frames or order thumbnails as a grid. Blackmagic gives no further detail on these functions. Studio also gets “multiple scripting API improvements”, and the Fusion tool and scripting reference documents are updated in both editions.

Media, OGraf and render fixes

Blackmagic lists a long series of fixes that affect camera media and delivery. They address slow loading of media from XDCAM drives, flashing media offline frames with some H.265 clips, a crash when decoding some multi-channel DNG files, file size estimates for spanned RED clips and artifacts in Sony XAVC Long GOP MXF renders. On Windows, the update fixes HE-AAC decoding of some clips and a GPU memory error with some OpenFX. ACES 2.0 artifacts on Windows and Linux are also fixed.

OGraf templates now load from network and zipped paths, and Blackmagic has addressed render timeouts and memory use with OGraf files. Other fixes cover the data burn scaling for render resolutions, render in place handles for frame-based formats, a hang when editing MultiText keyframes during render cache, missing Text+ inspector controls in older projects, an anchoring issue with Text+ CLS box extend controls, CustomTool LUT name controls, and network paths with accented characters on macOS 27. Studio users also get fixes for OpenFX that disappeared from MultiMaster trim groups on reload and for a render crash with MainConcept H.265 CRF encoding.

The standalone Fusion Studio 21.2 has its own list. The OGraf inspector now shows up to 35 template properties, and the update fixes OGraf loading and render issues, a material viewer crash with software rendering, the Shake random seed, script issues with the AddTool and SetInput functions, and the reading of video files with FFmpeg.

Before you install

The project library warning from the earlier 21.x releases still applies. Libraries stay compatible with DaVinci Resolve 20.3.2, but any project you create or open in 21.2 no longer opens in 20.3.2. Blackmagic recommends a full library backup and individual project backups before you update.

System requirements are the same as in 21.1: macOS 15 Sequoia or later on Apple silicon, Windows 10 Creators Update, Windows 11 for Arm on Snapdragon X Elite or NVIDIA RTX Spark, and Rocky Linux 8.6. NVIDIA users need Studio driver 581.57 or newer on Windows, 616.0 or newer on RTX Spark and 580.119.02 or newer on Linux. Monitoring through Blackmagic video hardware needs Desktop Video 12.9 or later.

Price and availability

DaVinci Resolve 21.2, DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 and Fusion Studio 21.2 are free downloads from the Blackmagic Design support center. The full release notes are available for the free version and for DaVinci Resolve Studio. DaVinci Resolve Studio is a one-time license at $295, which Blackmagic currently sells for $239 until November 20, 2026. More information is on the DaVinci Resolve product page.

Do you plan to grade or edit on a touch screen MacBook Pro, or do you stay with the keyboard and a control panel? And is Gen 6 color science already part of your workflow? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Steve Yedlin and Rian Johnson Release Chromagraph Camera – Film Color Pipeline for iPhone Stills, Grain, Halation and a RAW Gallery
entry.summary: Cinematographer Steve Yedlin ASC, director Rian Johnson and color science programmer Eric Cameron have released Chromagraph Camera, a still photo app for iPhone. The app skips Apple’s own look processing and builds each image from raw sensor data with the same custom color math t
entry.content:
Cinematographer Steve Yedlin ASC, director Rian Johnson and color science programmer Eric Cameron have released Chromagraph Camera, a still photo app for iPhone. The app skips Apple’s own look processing and builds each image from raw sensor data with the same custom color math that Yedlin uses on his feature films, including grain and halation. The gallery keeps full-quality scene-linear originals and applies the look non-destructively, and the app costs $12.99 / €14.99 as a one-time purchase. Let’s take a closer look.

Yedlin and Johnson have worked together since Johnson’s debut feature “Brick,” and their collaboration includes “Looper,” “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” and the three “Knives Out” films. Yedlin is also known for his long-form demos on how the look of an image comes from its preparation for display, not from the camera brand. In an Instagram post, he describes Chromagraph Camera as “simply the camera, image processing, and gallery app that we wanted for ourselves,” which the team now sells publicly on the App Store. According to the App Store listing, the app went live on October 20, 2026, and the public announcement followed a week later. Within days of the announcement, the app reportedly reached the top position in the Photo & Video category of the US App Store.

We have previously reported on iPhone camera apps aimed at filmmakers, such as Blackmagic Camera for iOS 3.5, Final Cut Camera 2.4, Kino and, more recently, Log Cam and RAW Cam. Those apps focus on video and give the user manual control over capture. Chromagraph Camera takes a different approach: it is a stills-only app with one curated look, and the controls sit after the shot, not before it.

Not a filter

The central claim of the app is that it is not a filter. According to the developer, Chromatic Applications LLC, a filter sits on top of the processing that the phone has already done, while Chromagraph starts from raw sensor data and “builds the image its own way.” Yedlin writes that the app “completely bypasses the iPhone look management and replaces it with the same custom math I use on all my films, tailored to Apple camera behavior.” In his own post on X, Rian Johnson summarized it in a similar way: the app shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone’s look processing, and uses the same image processing that the team uses on their movies.

Yedlin calls the look “opinionated.” In his words, it is “the nuanced and idiosyncratic rendering of tonality and chromaticity (as well as grain and halation)” that he, Johnson and Cameron like. The app does not offer a choice of film stock emulations or a library of presets. There is one core look, and the user adjusts it.

This is also the practical side of an argument that Yedlin has made publicly for years. In his Display Prep Demo and the companion essay “On Color Science for Filmmakers” (2016), he states that color rendition, highlight rolloff, halation and other perceptual attributes come mostly from the mathematical preparation of the image for display, not from the camera format. In that essay, he limits the argument to high-quality capture formats and names smartphone cameras as an example of inferior acquisition devices. Chromagraph Camera now applies the same type of display preparation to iPhone raw data.

Shoot first, see the look after

The capture process is closer to a film camera than to a typical phone app. The viewfinder shows the framing, but the finished look appears only after the image is processed. The user takes the picture and then opens the gallery to see it with the Chromagraph look applied. The App Store screenshots show a simple camera screen with a shutter button, a switch between the front and rear cameras, a timer, and 0.5x, 1x and 4x lens buttons. Version 1.2.2, released on November 4, adds optional grid lines and a level in the viewfinder, plus manual aperture control on the 1x camera of the iPhone 18 Pro models.

Chromagraph is a stills-only camera. According to the App Store listing, it does not record video.

A gallery that keeps scene-linear originals

The gallery stores full-quality raw files. Yedlin specifies that these are scene-linear originals, and the app applies the look and the user’s own adjustments live for viewing. All edits stay non-destructive, so the user can change them later.

For sharing, the app exports smaller files with the look baked in, either to the iOS photo library or directly to friends. An auto-export option in Preferences sends every photo to the photo library right after capture, as a JPEG or HEIC file with the look applied.

Grading controls within the core look

The editor has four sections: Tone, Color, Texture and Crop. The App Store screenshots show the Texture section with separate Grain and Halation tabs. Grain has sliders for amplitude and grain size, plus a “Force Pixel Size Grain” switch. The editor also shows capture metadata such as shutter speed, aperture, ISO and white balance in Kelvin.

According to Yedlin, these “grading knobs” allow “pretty dramatic adjustments while keeping within that overall core look.” The developer describes the tools as intuitive yet powerful controls for color, tone and texture that keep every image true to the look at the core of the app.

If you want more background on why halation is part of so many film-emulation tools, read our article “Chasing the Glow”. On the professional side, we recently covered ARRI Film Lab 1.5, which also adds grain and halation in post.

Who is behind it?

The app comes from Chromatic Applications LLC. The company’s website says that it makes “software to empower filmmakers in their visual authorship.” Next to Chromagraph, the website lists OFX plugins that package image processing algorithms used by Yedlin for DaVinci Resolve, Baselight, Nuke and other hosts, and a lighting control system called yLumination. The company gives no release dates or prices for these products. Yedlin was also part of the program at the IMAGO Oslo Digital Cinema Conference 2025.

Current limitations

Chromagraph Camera captures stills only, and there is no video mode. The look is a single, fixed design, and users who want a choice of film emulations or a neutral starting point will not find it here. The finished look is not visible in the viewfinder, only in the gallery after capture. The app is available only on the App Store, in English, and it needs iOS 17 or later. The developer does not publish a list of supported iPhone models or details about which raw format the app records. Since version 1.2.2, the app alerts users when a camera on their phone does not support raw capture. Statements about the image pipeline come from Yedlin and the developer.

Price and availability

Chromagraph Camera is available now on the App Store for $12.99 / €14.99 / £12.99 as a one-time purchase, with no subscription. It needs iOS 17 or later. The current version is 1.2.2, released on November 4, 2026. According to the developer’s privacy statement, the app does not collect or keep personal information. More information is on the Chromagraph website.

Would you give up control at capture for one curated look from Steve Yedlin’s pipeline? And do you shoot stills on your iPhone with the native camera, or with a third-party app? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Canon EOS C400, EOS C80 and EOS C50 Firmware Update Announced – Expanding Cinema EOS Capabilities
entry.summary: Canon has announced a new Cinema EOS firmware update for three cameras: the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50. It adds Multi-Matrix color control for camera matching and LED volume work, autofocus at more Slow & Fast frame rates, several broadcast and virtual production features, wi
entry.content:
Canon has announced a new Cinema EOS firmware update for three cameras: the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50. It adds Multi-Matrix color control for camera matching and LED volume work, autofocus at more Slow & Fast frame rates, several broadcast and virtual production features, wider button customization, and Speedlite flash support for the EOS C50. The update will be free to download from December 2026.

Canon says the new features respond to customer feedback and changing production needs. This is the latest in a series of firmware releases for these bodies. In June, Canon released firmware 1.0.4.1 for the EOS C50 and 1.0.6.1 for the EOS C80 and EOS C400, with USB external control and SRT reconnection. In August, the C80 and C400 gained Cinema Exposure Mode, AE Ramping Compensation, and support for the CN30x40 Cine-Servo. We have covered all three cameras in detail, from the EOS C400 announcement and our EOS C400 Lab Test, to the EOS C80 launch, EOS C80 review and mini-doc, and the EOS C50 announcement, EOS C50 review and EOS C50 Lab Test. Let’s take a look at what the December update brings.

Multi-Matrix for camera matching and LED volumes

The headline addition for all three cameras is Multi-Matrix Support. Canon describes it as advanced control over color and saturation on selected color axes. Multi-matrix controls are a standard tool on broadcast system cameras, where a shader adjusts individual hues to bring several cameras to the same look.

Canon positions the feature for two cases: matching multiple cameras, and shooting against LED volumes, where the camera has to work with the color pipeline of the wall and the real-time engine. According to the company, this helps the cameras fit into existing real-time color workflows. Canon has not yet said how many color axes are available, or whether Multi-Matrix can be adjusted from remote control software as well as from the camera menu.

What changes for broadcast and virtual production?

Canon lists several more additions for broadcast and virtual production work in the same section of the press release:

  • Improved CV metadata for focus and zoom encoder data
  • Black Level adjustment when shooting in Canon Log 2 or Canon Log 3
  • Image Stabilization support for lenses longer than 1000mm
  • Audio output in Slow & Fast mode

Better focus and zoom encoder data matters most for virtual production, where camera tracking systems and real-time engines use the lens position to match the virtual background to the physical lens. Black Level adjustment in Canon Log 2 and Canon Log 3 gives operators one more control when they match log images between cameras, which ties in with the Multi-Matrix addition.

Canon does not name specific lenses for the Image Stabilization change. The CINE-SERVO 40-1200mm T5.0-10.8, which Canon introduced in August, reaches 1200mm at its long end, so it is one current Canon lens in this range. Audio output in Slow & Fast mode is aimed at productions that switch between high-speed sports footage and post-match interviews without changing camera settings. The press release does not say which of these broadcast features apply to each of the three bodies, so the full release notes in December will be the reference.

More autofocus frame rates in Slow & Fast mode

For the EOS C400 and EOS C80, the update extends autofocus in Slow & Fast mode to more frame rates between 60 and 120p, including 72p, 75p, 90p and 96p. Canon says this brings its autofocus tracking to a wider range of slow-motion work, from narrative and documentary to commercials and music videos.

Canon also lists improved on-screen information, including Base ISO and fan indicators. Both the C400 and C80 use a 6K full-frame back-illuminated sensor with triple base ISO at 800, 3200 and 12800, so a direct display of the active base ISO makes it easier to confirm which sensitivity range the camera is in while shooting.

Speedlite flash support for the EOS C50

The EOS C50 gets support for compatible Canon Speedlite flash accessories through its Multi-Function Accessory Shoe. According to Canon, supported accessories include EL-series and EX-series Speedlites, Macro Lights and Speedlite Transmitters. The press release refers to a footnote for the full compatibility list but does not include it, so we recommend checking Canon’s support pages for the exact models once the firmware is out.

Canon aims this feature at photographers and hybrid shooters, such as wedding and event creators, who want flash stills and video from the same camera at the same event. The press release lists this feature for the EOS C50 only.

Customization of buttons and dials

All three cameras get more customization options for RF lens buttons, camera control dials and assignable buttons. Canon says users can assign a wider range of functions, including autofocus, the digital tele-converter, sensor mode, and exposure settings. According to the company, these changes were made in response to customer requests.

Price and availability

The firmware updates for the EOS C400, EOS C80 and EOS C50 will be available free of charge from December 2026 via Canon Europe support. At the time of writing, the EOS C50 body is listed at $3,699 / €3,297.82, the EOS C80 body at $5,599 / €4,222.48, and the EOS C400 body at $8,799 / €7,257.84.

Which of these additions matters most for your work: Multi-Matrix for camera matching, autofocus at 90p and 96p, or flash support on the C50? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Sony RIALTO 65 Explained – Single 65mm Sensor, Universal Lens Mount, Full-Frame Modes Coming
entry.summary: Last week, I was at Pinewood Studios in London for Sony’s RIALTO 65 event, and I sat down with Sony’s Sebastian Leske to go through the new 65mm camera extension for the VENICE 2. We talked about the sensor, the missing lens mount, future crop modes, recording times, and the pric
entry.content:
Last week, I was at Pinewood Studios in London for Sony’s RIALTO 65 event, and I sat down with Sony’s Sebastian Leske to go through the new 65mm camera extension for the VENICE 2. We talked about the sensor, the missing lens mount, future crop modes, recording times, and the price, which Sony now confirms at €72,000.

The RIALTO 65 is not a new camera body. It is a 65mm format sensor head that replaces the full-frame sensor block of an existing VENICE 2, either on a cable or attached directly to the body. We covered the official specifications in our RIALTO 65 announcement article, so this piece is mostly about the answers that a spec sheet does not give you: why Sony made certain decisions, what is still missing at launch, and who the system is really for. You can watch our full conversation in the video below.

The event took place at Sony’s Digital Motion Picture Centre at Pinewood, the studio complex that many people know as the home of the 007 films. I have been there many times over the years, and (sadly) never for a 007 shoot, always for Sony. Sony first teased the RIALTO 65 at Cine Gear 2026 and published a short development announcement at that time. At Pinewood, it was finally a working unit with real footage, and Sony had a long table of 65mm and large-format lenses ready for guests to test.

A project that started with DPs

Sebastian told me that the RIALTO 65 started long before Cine Gear. Sony gets constant feedback from cinematographers, and according to him, many DPs told Sony something like this: “We love the VENICE 2, we love full frame, but we would like to have the 65mm look in the same camera.” Sony had seen how many productions shot on the VENICE 2, and it also saw how many films were shot in 65mm, on film and digitally.

Sebastian also explained why it took time. For the Cinema Line, Sony wants the image quality to speak for itself, so the team worked on dynamic range, latitude, skin tones, and highlight roll-off before it was ready to talk about the product. A second goal was a color match with the VENICE and VENICE 2. In practice, this means that a production can shoot 65mm on the A camera and use a regular VENICE 2 as the B camera, without two different color pipelines.

One sensor, not a stitched one

My first technical question was about the sensor itself. Sebastian confirmed that it is a completely new, single sensor developed for the 65mm system, and not a stitched design. It measures 53.75 x 35.83mm, with a diagonal of about 65mm. According to Sony, it is the largest sensor built into a digital cinema camera so far.

Sebastian placed it in Sony’s own history. Nine years ago, the original VENICE moved Sony’s high-end cinema cameras from Super 35 to full frame. The RIALTO 65 is the next step up, to what photographers would call medium format. We also talked briefly about that terminology problem, because “65mm”, “large format”, and “medium format” mean slightly different things in photography and in filmmaking.

The resolution goes up only a little compared to the VENICE 2 8K, to 9.6K, while the sensor area is about 2.2 times larger than full frame. So the photosites are much larger, and that is where the second base ISO of 10000 comes from. The first base ISO is 2500. During the interview, I said that an ISO 10000 base puts it almost in FX3 and FX6 territory, which is very unusual for a sensor of this size. Sony rates the latitude at 15+ stops at ISO 2500. We will of course check that claim in our lab as soon as we get a unit, and we will compare it with our VENICE 2 Lab Test. Rolling shutter on a 9.6K sensor of this size is the first number I want to see.

Why 3:2 matters

The part Sebastian talked about most was the shape. ARRI’s ALEXA 65 and the newer ALEXA 265 have a sensor of a similar width, but with a much wider aspect ratio. The RIALTO 65 is 3:2, which adds a lot of height. Sebastian said that this extra height is what DPs were looking for. For the 65mm system, as he put it, “it’s the canvas” that cinematographers paint on.

In practice, the 3:2 frame gives room for anamorphic capture, for wide landscapes, and for framing that needs to serve several deliverables. With a sensor this large, the shallow depth of field also helps to separate an actor from the background, even in a wide shot. Sony supports anamorphic lenses with de-squeeze display at multiple ratios and a Zoom to Fit function, so the operator can see the correct composition on the monitor.

How the RIALTO 65 fits on a VENICE 2

The hardware logic follows the VENICE Extension System Mini, which I also saw at Pinewood when Sony introduced it. You take the full-frame sensor block out of the VENICE 2, store it safely, and attach the RIALTO 65 to the body. On a cable, this is Extension Mode. Attached directly, it becomes one camera in Studio Mode.

Sebastian described how the system grew. The original Rialto took the sensor out of the VENICE so that the camera could go into tight places or onto gimbals. Then users asked for something even smaller, and Sony built the Mini without the internal ND mechanism. The RIALTO 65 is a mix of both. Size-wise, it reminds me more of the original Rialto, simply because the sensor is so much larger, and the head weighs about 1.5kg (3.3lb). But like the Mini, it comes with its own sensor, because there is no 65mm VENICE to take one from.

A 4.5m (14.8ft) cable is included, and a 12m (39.4ft) cable is available as an option. The cable detaches at both the head and the body, which makes rigging easier. The head also records tilt and roll as metadata for post-production, which is useful for VFX work.

Drop-in ND instead of a rotary ND

I asked why Sony went with drop-in ND filters instead of the rotary ND of the VENICE. Sebastian said that the larger sensor does not leave room for the rotary mechanism if the head is to stay compact. Sony also wanted the head to match the design of the VENICE 2 body when it is attached in Studio Mode. The system comes with 11 drop-in ND filters that have electronic contacts, so the VENICE 2 automatically reads the density of the filter that is in the head. A spare kit with the same 11 filters will be available, but Sony does not sell single filters.

Why there is no lens mount

This was the part I found most interesting. The RIALTO 65 ships without a lens mount. The original Rialto and the VENICE 2 have an E-mount with a PL adapter, but Sebastian explained that E-mount is too small to cover the full 65mm sensor. So Sony uses a universal mount interface instead.

Third-party companies already make LPL mounts for the Rialto and the VENICE 2, and Sony’s view is that they have the experience to update those adapters for the 65mm system. Rental houses can then select brand A or brand B, or even develop their own mount. At Pinewood, the unit had an LPL mount, with LPL-to-PL adapters on hand. In theory, Sebastian confirmed, this means mounts for almost any lens can be made. With a lens and adapter that support data communication, the system records focal length, focus position, and aperture as metadata for editing, VFX, and virtual production. There is no autofocus, which is no surprise for a camera in this class, and Sebastian confirmed that there is none even in a cropped mode.

Which lenses cover the sensor?

Sony brought many lenses to the event so that guests could check coverage for themselves. According to Sebastian, some lenses cover the 2.20:1 mode, and some cover the full Open Gate. He said that it is interesting for Sony, and for the lens makers, to see which lenses cover fully, which cover partially, and by how much. He also expects that more lens manufacturers will come to Sony to test their glass on the RIALTO 65.

The numbers give a good guide here. The 2.20:1 mode has a diagonal of about 59mm, while the full Open Gate needs about 65mm. Large-format lenses such as the ZEISS Panoptes 65 primes and the Angénieux EZ 65 zooms cover an image circle of about 60mm, which fits the 2.20:1 mode. For the full 3:2 frame, you need glass that is made for true 65mm coverage.

My feeling is that this will play out like it did with the FUJIFILM GFX ETERNA 55. At first, people said there were not enough lenses, and then more and more lens makers started to support the format. An open mount makes that much easier, because you are not limited to one mount from the start.

Full frame and Super 35 come later

At launch, the RIALTO 65 has two sensor modes: 9.6K Open Gate in 3:2, and 9.6K 2.20:1. If you want full frame today, Sebastian’s advice is to put the original VENICE 2 sensor back in, or to shoot Open Gate with frame lines and crop in post. Sony is working on additional sensor modes, including full frame and Super 35, for a later firmware update, similar to the many modes on the VENICE 2. A full-frame mode on this sensor would land at about 6K to 7K, according to Sebastian. For a production that wants one camera for everything, these modes are important, so I hope Sony does not keep them on the roadmap for too long.

Same X-OCN, same cards

I have heard many promises of sensor upgrades for existing cameras over the years, and very often they did not happen, because the processing in the older body was not fast enough, or because it needed more power. So I asked Sebastian how the VENICE 2 deals with the extra resolution, and whether there is a new version of X-OCN.

His answer: nothing changes. The RIALTO 65 records the same X-OCN flavors (ST, XT, and LT) in 16-bit to the same AXS cards, with S-Log3 and S-Gamut3. The format can handle the full Open Gate without problems. Recording times go down a little, but Sebastian said that a 1TB card in X-OCN ST still holds about half an hour. For a rental house, that means no new media, no new card readers, and no change for the DIT.

Why there is no RIALTO 65 camera package

Here I pushed back a little. ARRI sells dedicated 65mm cameras. With Sony, you always need a VENICE 2 with a full-frame sensor first, and then you add the RIALTO 65. I asked Sebastian why Sony does not offer a single 65mm camera package (Sony, I would still like to see one).

His answer makes sense for rental houses. Every VENICE 2 in a fleet, 6K or 8K, bought yesterday or four years ago, can take the RIALTO 65. A rental house does not need to buy a whole new camera that might go out on only 10 percent of its jobs. For the camera assistant, the DIT, and the data wrangler, the menus, formats, and tools stay the same. Sebastian called the VENICE 2 the center of the platform: one body, with Super 35, full frame, and now 65mm as options. I agree that this is a strong argument for owners of a VENICE 2 fleet. For a production that only wants to rent a 65mm camera, the package question matters less, because the rental house puts the system together anyway.

Price and availability

The RIALTO 65 ships in the first half of 2027. Sebastian confirmed a list price of €72,000 for the RIALTO 65 alone, and about €138,000 together with a VENICE 2. That means the 65mm head costs a bit more than the VENICE 2 body it connects to. B&H lists the RIALTO 65 at $80,000, and CVP has a product page without a price (but it will be €72,000). The optional ND filter kit and the 12m cable also arrive in the first half of 2027. For more information, please visit the Sony website.

The footage I saw at Pinewood looked beautiful, and I am very curious to test the RIALTO 65 in our lab. Would you rent a 65mm head for your VENICE 2 rather than a dedicated 65mm camera? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Inside PIXBOOM – Factory Tour of the “Spark” High-Speed Camera in China
entry.summary: Recently, I packed my bag in Japan and flew to Shenzhen, China to visit PIXBOOM, the young company behind the Spark high-speed camera. I visited the factory in Dongguan, where the camera is assembled and tested, and learned about a new production line that will start operating so
entry.content:
Recently, I packed my bag in Japan and flew to Shenzhen, China to visit PIXBOOM, the young company behind the Spark high-speed camera. I visited the factory in Dongguan, where the camera is assembled and tested, and learned about a new production line that will start operating soon. I was also kindly invited to see the unique office in Shenzhen and meet the people behind this company. Here is my report, guys, and I hope you enjoy the journey as much as I did.

My trip started at Osaka’s Kansai Airport. Shenzhen has become one of the most important places in the world for technology and electronics manufacturing, and it is also home to PIXBOOM. By now, I am sure most of you know the company by now, its first camera being the PIXBOOM Spark, a compact Super 35 high-speed camera with a backside-illuminated (BSI) global shutter sensor, up to 1,000 fps in 4K and continuous RAW recording to a removable SSD. The idea behind it is simple: bring extreme slow motion to filmmakers who could never justify renting a traditional high-speed package. I wanted to meet the people behind this idea, and see how the camera is actually made.

We at CineD have been covering the Spark’s journey from the very beginning. We reported about the Kickstarter launch at IBC 2025, where the camera also won a CineD Best-of-Show Award. We then took a beta unit to India for our first hands-on review, and my colleague Gunther shot a wildlife documentary in Goa with it. Later we reported on the first production unit, the start of shipping in May, and the latest firmware updates. But we wanted to go deeper, and so we decided to see where the camera is born – the factory floor.

From a research lab to a Kickstarter success

The PIXBOOM company story started in a research lab. Its co-founders, Dr. Huang and Dr. Chengyang, were PhD students working on ultra-high-speed imaging systems for scientific use, capable of capturing millions of frames per second. In 2015, they set out to make high-speed imaging accessible to a much wider group of creators, and over the years they moved from lab experiments to real-world prototypes, refined with feedback from filmmakers. You can read the company’s own account of that journey on its Spark history page.

The camera made quite an impression before it even reached the market. During its Kickstarter campaign, PIXBOOM raised around $3.5 million, and to be honest, it is not hard to see why.

Why is the factory in Dongguan?

My first question was a practical one: why is the factory so far from the center of town? The answer was very straightforward: Shenzhen is often called China’s Silicon Valley, but the manufacturing usually happens in the neighboring city of Dongguan. “Everybody just knows the good factories are usually based in Dongguan,” I was told. So off we went. After meeting the core team in the factory offices, I finally saw the place where the Spark is made.

Quality control for a camera that runs hot

A high-speed camera pushes a huge amount of data through its electronics, so I was curious how quality control works here. The team explained that the Spark goes through the usual checks of any electronic product: basic signals, image quality, calibration, and sensor adjustments. “But for high speed, one important point is the cooling.” Every camera goes through a strict high-temperature test in the factory, running continuously in a heat chamber for cycles of several hours. “If it survives this test, it can be shipped.”

The Spark uses active cooling with intake and exhaust vents, and PIXBOOM rates it for operation between 0°C and 40°C (32°F to 104°F). A camera designed to be rigged on cars, robotic arms, and gimbals has to keep working, even under direct sunlight. These heat tests ensure that it can handle these conditions before it leaves the building.

What does a BSI sensor do for slow motion?

I asked the team to explain why they decided on a BSI sensor. BSI stands for backside illumination. It is a semiconductor process that flips the wafer, so light reaches the photodiode from the back side, and this improves the light efficiency of each pixel. “For high-speed video or slow motion, one important issue is the light demand,” I was told. “BSI improves the light efficiency to get brighter footage under the same lighting conditions.”

Anyone who has ever shot at 1,000 fps knows the problem: every frame gets only a tiny slice of exposure time, so light is always the first thing that runs out. The company says the Spark needs only about 25% of the light a typical high-speed setup calls for, and that the BSI design increases quantum efficiency from around 60% to more than 80%. For slow motion in real locations, every bit of extra sensitivity counts.

The compromises of a first camera

Going from concept to finished product is a long journey, and the final result often looks what a little different from what you originally had in mind. So, I asked whether the team had to compromise anywhere, and the answer was honest. “Because we are a start-up company and Spark is our first camera, we need to focus on the main mission of this camera, which is to bring a good slow-motion camera to our creators”, I was told by Dr. Huang.

That means no audio and no autofocus. Autofocus is relatively complex, and according to the team, feedback from users also played a role in that decision. On audio, the explanation was clear: “To add audio into Spark is easy. But to make it fully usable and 100% perfect is difficult. Audio is a very deep and large field.” In my opinion, as a documentary shooter who always records sound, this is a decision that some people will miss. (The camera can shoot at 24/25 fps too.) At the same time, slow-motion footage is very rarely used with its original sound, and a focused product is often a better first product. I’ll let you guys decide for yourselves, as everyone works a bit differently.

An empty hall that will soon be busy

When I asked where the company sees itself in three years, and whether PIXBOOM will still be making only one camera, the answer was short: “We will have more…”

Then Dr. Huang, PIXBOOM’s CTO, showed me a large, empty hall. “It’s empty now, but it will be very busy in one or two months,” he said. “This is a new factory line for our PIXBOOM camera. We are trying to get people, devices, and instruments here to build a new line for the Spark camera.” Looking at the empty workstations, it was easy to imagine how this space would look when it is full of workers and products.

Back in Shenzhen: the people behind the product

After a quick lunch, we drove back to Shenzhen, a city of nearly 18 million people that has grown from a small fishing town into one of China’s leading tech hubs in just a few decades. Skyscrapers, busy highways, and technology are everywhere you look. The PIXBOOM offices, however, are a very unique space.

I asked Jing Qi, PIXBOOM’s Chief Marketing Officer, about the concept behind the space. At the beginning, she said, the team was very small, and everyone had to do multiple jobs to get the company off the ground. “But at the same time, we need to consider how to make people comfortable, so they enjoy staying and working here,” she explained. “It’s a space where we spend more than eight hours a day.” Jing doesn’t see herself in the classic marketing role. “I treat myself like a bridge,” she told me, “between the company and filmmakers, between me and my team, and between cultures. So my role is to break the boundaries.”

Spark specs at a glance

For those of you who don’t know the Spark camera, here is a short summary: It uses a 14.2MP Super 35 global shutter BSI CMOS sensor (25.34 x 16.90mm) with 4.6K 3:2 open gate resolution (4608 x 3072), dual native ISO with settings from 400 to 1600, and 13 stops of dynamic range, according to PIXBOOM. Top frame rates in PIXBOOM RAW are 670 fps at 4.6K open gate, 887 fps at 4K 16:9, and 2,182 fps at 2K 2.37:1, with custom resolutions that go higher still. The camera currently records 10-bit RAW, and 12-bit RAW is in development.

Recording goes to the removable 2.5TB PIXBOOM Pro Card at up to 10GB/s, so record time is limited only by card capacity. The card offloads directly via USB-C at 20Gbps, without a card reader. The all-aluminum body weighs about 1.1kg (2.42lb) and measures 108 x 110 x 130mm (4.25 x 4.33 x 5.12in). It integrates a 3.5-inch 6.22M-dot touchscreen, a V-Lock battery plate, 12G-SDI and HDMI 2.0 outputs (both 4K 60p), a 9-pin EXT port, and Wi-Fi control. Interchangeable locking adapters are available for E, EF, and PL mount. Genlock, timecode, and some remote features are still under development and will need future firmware or the upcoming I/O expansion accessory.

Price and availability

The PIXBOOM Spark is shipping now. The package includes the camera body, a 2.5TB PIXBOOM Pro Card, and one mount adapter (E, EF, or PL), in silver or black. B&H lists it at $13,999, and CVP lists it at €12,749.95 (excluding VAT). Additional mount adapters cost $599 each, and an extra 2.5TB Pro Card costs $2,999. Retailer stock varies by mount and color, so check the listing for your configuration.

PIXBOOM is still early in its journey, but that is exactly what makes it so interesting. What I saw was a young company with big ambitions and a lot of energy, trying to carve out its own place in the world of cinema cameras. I am curious to see where they go from here.

Many thanks to: Dr. Huang, CTO; Chengyang Hu, Founder and CEO; Jing Qi, Chief Marketing Officer; Xin Tang, Supply Chain Director; Wong Haoyuan, Head of Visual Design; Max Zhai, Head of R&D; Daisy Wu, Senior Project Manager; Vicky Wen, Head of Customer Service Center; Ariel Levesque, PIXBOOM Spark footage; Little Beauty, Chief Pet Officer; and the entire PIXBOOM team!

What do you think about the PIXBOOM Spark and the idea of owning a high-speed camera instead of renting one? Would audio or autofocus matter to you in a camera like this? Please share your thoughts with us in the comment section below!

entry.title: Nikon ZR Firmware 2.00 Detailed – Log3G10 in H.265, Selectable High ISO NR and 3D LUT over HDMI
entry.summary: Nikon has published the full feature list of firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, the first major update for its RED-developed full-frame cinema camera. The update brings Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB to H.265 recording, a selectable High ISO NR level, more assignable controls,
entry.content:
Nikon has published the full feature list of firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, the first major update for its RED-developed full-frame cinema camera. The update brings Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB to H.265 recording, a selectable High ISO NR level, more assignable controls, focus peaking with a LUT applied in R3D NE, 3D LUT output over HDMI, and a fix for black-level flicker in low light. Nikon says the firmware is scheduled to be available before the end of the year, but it still gives no exact date.

The Nikon ZR has been on the market since October 2025, and its firmware history so far is short. Version 1.10 arrived in January 2026 with wired timecode sync, RED file naming and more, and version 1.11 in March fixed two bugs. In August, we reported that Nikon ZR owners were still waiting for a big firmware update, and in September, Nikon made the development announcement for firmware V2.00 with three confirmed features. The announcement of November 3 adds several items to that list. Let’s take a look at what it includes.

RED color science in a smaller file

The main change is a new tone mode option for H.265 recording. Until now, Log3G10 was not available for H.265 recording. With firmware 2.00, Log3G10 gamma and the REDWideGamutRGB color gamut are also available when the camera records H.265. According to Nikon, this gives footage in the compact H.265 format “the high color-grading latitude made possible by RED color science, with its smooth tonal gradation and exceptionally wide color gamut.”

For productions that do not need RAW on every shot, this means one Log3G10 color pipeline for both R3D NE and H.265 material, with much smaller files from the second. LUTs built for Log3G10, such as the Phantom LUTs for the Nikon ZR, target the same curve. H.265 on the ZR stays a 10-bit 4:2:0 codec, and Nikon has not said whether the update changes its processing.

Four levels of High ISO NR

The second feature from the development announcement is a selectable [High ISO NR] level. Nikon lists four settings, available when the camera records H.265 with Log3G10 or N-Log. The company describes the range as going “from shooting that prioritizes inherent textures to shooting that calls for smooth rendering with minimal noise.” Nikon gives no further details on what each level does. In September, we noted that this setting matches how the Nikon Z6III already handles high ISO noise reduction in H.265.

Another image processing change was not in the September announcement. Nikon says new processing “suppresses frame-by-frame fluctuations in black level, reducing flicker that tends to occur in low-light conditions and in dark areas of the frame.” The press release does not say which recording formats this applies to.

More assignable controls

Firmware 2.00 also extends the customization options. ISO sensitivity, exposure settings, white balance (WB) and white balance color temperature (WBK) can now be assigned to the command dials. In addition, [3D LUT/View Assist] can be assigned to an Fn button, so the operator can switch between the two with one press. Nikon’s position is that these changes let the operator adjust settings “without taking their eyes off the monitor.”

Monitoring: focus peaking in R3D NE and LUTs over HDMI

The third feature from September is focus peaking during R3D NE recording. The missing focus peaking in R3D NE was one of the most frequent owner complaints we listed in August, and one of the gaps that reviewers, us included in our Nikon ZR review, pointed out at launch. In the final wording, Nikon says focus peaking is now supported “even when a 3D LUT is applied during recording in R3D NE format.”

The ZR can also apply a 3D LUT to its HDMI video output. This lets an external monitor or a director’s monitor show a rendering close to the graded image, without loading the LUT on the monitor itself. The camera has a micro-HDMI port, and accessories such as the SmallRig micro-HDMI to HDMI adapter are made to protect that connection on a rig.

What is still missing

Open Gate recording and a desqueeze display for anamorphic lenses are not part of firmware 2.00. In its September announcement, Nikon said it is developing both features “with the goal of incorporating them in ZR firmware in 2027.” Several other requests from owners are also not in the November list, among them internal false color, an exposure meter in R3D NE, more compressed R3D NE options, and a lighter 10-bit 4:2:2 codec than ProRes 422 HQ. Third-party tools such as the ZR CTL control app continue to fill some of these gaps. In September, Nikon also said that RED is updating its RED CONTROL and RED CONTROL PRO apps to support the ZR.

Price and availability

Nikon says firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR is “scheduled to be available before the end of the year,” with no exact release date. The Nikon ZR body is available at B&H for $2,196.95 and at CVP for €1,804.69.

Are you a Nikon ZR owner, and which of these features will you use first? Is Log3G10 in H.265 enough for you, or are you waiting for Open Gate in 2027? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: DJI Osmo Pocket 4P Firmware V01.02.1149 Released – 18x Zoom, Smoother Lens Switching and Scene Presets
entry.summary: DJI has released firmware V01.02.1149 for the Osmo Pocket 4P, and it is the biggest update the dual-camera pocket gimbal has received so far. The roughly 1.1GB download raises the maximum zoom from 12x to 18x, improves ActiveTrack and the 60mm telephoto camera, adds Stage and Sun
entry.content:
DJI has released firmware V01.02.1149 for the Osmo Pocket 4P, and it is the biggest update the dual-camera pocket gimbal has received so far. The roughly 1.1GB download raises the maximum zoom from 12x to 18x, improves ActiveTrack and the 60mm telephoto camera, adds Stage and Sunset scene presets, and promises smoother transitions between the two cameras. That last point is the one I was waiting for, because it targets the exposure jump at 3x. First owner reports say it is better now, but not fixed for everyone.

The Osmo Pocket 4P is a camera that our team has spent a lot of time with. It pairs a 20mm-equivalent f/2.0 wide camera on a 1-inch LOFIC sensor with a 60mm-equivalent f/1.8 medium telephoto camera on a 1/1.28-inch sensor. We reported on the European launch of the Osmo Pocket 4P in July, and in our DJI Osmo Pocket 4P Lab Test (yes, that is my face in the latitude shots), the wide camera measured 16 stops of dynamic range at SNR = 2, the best result we have ever recorded. In August, DJI added cloud uploads and D-Log for slow motion. The new firmware goes much further. Let’s look at what it brings.

18x zoom, but only 3x is optical

The headline number is the new maximum zoom in photo and video modes: 18x instead of 12x, which is approximately 360mm in full-frame terms. Let’s be clear about what that means. Only the step from the 20mm wide camera to the 60mm telephoto camera is optical, and that gives you 3x. Everything above 3x is a crop of the telephoto sensor and, at the higher factors, an upscale of a small part of it. I would not expect 18x to give usable images for professional work, and my guess is that DJI added it mainly for the spec sheet and for social media clips.

The zoom changes that matter more to me are less visible. DJI says the telephoto camera now gives better image quality and sharpness in 4K/30p, and that zooming is smoother. Owners have already noticed one side effect: a long press on the zoom button now runs all the way to 18x, and there is no setting to stop it at a chosen factor. (DJI, a zoom limit in the menu would be a small change with a big effect. Please add it in the next update.)

The exposure jump at 3x: partly fixed

According to the changelog, transitions between the two camera modules during a zoom should now look more natural. This is the fix many Osmo Pocket 4P owners asked for. Since launch, the camera has shown a clear jump in brightness when it switches from the wide to the telephoto camera. That is not a big surprise, because the two cameras are different systems. In our lab test, the wide camera recorded D-Log 2 at a native ISO of 1600, and the telephoto camera recorded D-Log at a native ISO of 400.

First user reports on Reddit and Facebook are mixed. Several owners say that the jump in D-Log is gone, but only at ISO 400, the lowest ISO of the telephoto camera. Others say the jump is now approximately 1/3 stop, compared to one to two stops before. Some still see a visible change in brightness. My feeling is that DJI has improved the exposure match at specific settings, and not across the full ISO range. That is only my guess, though, so if a seamless zoom through 3x is important for your shoot, test it before you rely on it.

More ISO range in D-Log, according to users

Some changes are not in the official list. Several owners report that D-Log now starts at ISO 100 instead of ISO 400. D-Log 2 seems to get an Auto ISO option with a selectable range for the first time, but that range starts at ISO 400. DJI has not confirmed this. A lower ISO in D-Log is useful in bright sun when you do not have ND filters with you. Keep in mind that our lab results are for the native ISO settings, so we cannot yet say what ISO 100 does to the dynamic range of the telephoto camera.

Tracking, HDR and live output

DJI has also improved the performance and stability of ActiveTrack, the tracking function in which the gimbal keeps a selected subject in the frame. According to the release notes, the update also gives:

  • Steadier gimbal stabilization
  • Better image quality for Wi-Fi livestreams, the DisplayPort output and webcam mode
  • Better results in HDR scenes when portrait mode is off
  • Improved HDR playback on the camera screen

The livestream and webcam improvements show that DJI sees the Pocket 4P as more than a vlogging camera. It is also a small streaming and video call camera. DJI does not say how much the image quality of these outputs has changed, so I will not guess a number here.

Scene presets, Intelligent Highlight and file access

Two new scene presets, Stage and Sunset, adjust the camera settings automatically. A stage mode is also part of the Insta360 Luna Ultra firmware update with 15x zoom from September. I don’t think that is a coincidence: both companies now compete for concert footage, and both use long digital zoom ranges to do it. Intelligent Highlight finds highlight moments automatically during recording. Users can also mark highlights during playback and share them through the DJI Mimo app.

The other additions are about getting files off the camera:

  • Auto Media Transfer: photos and Live Photos can move to the smartphone automatically after capture.
  • Huawei Direct Transfer: owners of Huawei devices with HarmonyOS 6.1 or later can transfer footage from playback with one tap.
  • File access when off: the camera now connects by USB to a computer or an OTG-capable smartphone when it is switched off. In sleep mode, users can view and download footage through DJI Mimo.

For me, file access in the off state is the most practical change in this list. The camera no longer has to be switched on to show its 103GB of internal storage to a computer, which removes a small but frequent step at the end of every shoot day.

How to install the update

Firmware V01.02.1149 is free and available now through the DJI Mimo app. When we performed the update, we did not see it in the settings menu and could only find it on the start page of the app instead.

I also recommend a hard reset after the installation: hold the power button for 10 seconds to restart the camera.

DJI’s product and download pages are not available from the US, where the Osmo Pocket 4P is still not officially sold.

Price and availability

The Osmo Pocket 4P is available in Europe, the UK, Canada and Australia. DJI lists the Standard Combo at €599 and the Vlog Combo at €689, including VAT, on the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P product page. CVP lists the Standard Combo at €515.35 and the Vlog Combo at €588.98, excluding VAT. B&H does not list the camera, because it is not sold in the US.

Have you installed the new firmware on your Osmo Pocket 4P, and is the exposure jump at 3x gone on your camera? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: SmallRig x CineD OrBrella Crowdfunding Ends November 8 – Last Chance to Get the Campaign Price
entry.summary: Guys, this is the final week! The crowdfunding campaign for our SmallRig x CineD OrBrella soft light closes on November 8, 2026. After that, the 60W bi-color umbrella light will cost $80 more. So, if you were still on the fence about it, now is the last chance to grab it and save
entry.content:
Guys, this is the final week! The crowdfunding campaign for our SmallRig x CineD OrBrella soft light closes on November 8, 2026. After that, the 60W bi-color umbrella light will cost $80 more. So, if you were still on the fence about it, now is the last chance to grab it and save some money!

I can’t believe how fast these weeks went… It feels like yesterday that I stood at the SmallRig booth at IBC 2026 and watched all 200 early-bird units go in three days. The light also won a Future Best of Show Award at the show. If you missed the backstory, our launch article explains how the idea came about, and the crowdfunding article covers the IBC story and the full feature set. We also talked about it at length on Focus Check ep133. As the crowdfunding campaign is ending this week, I quickly wanted to remind you guys and also tell you why I think this light is useful. Keep reading to find out what you get if you back it before the campaign ends on November 8th.

Soft light in 15 seconds

For so long, my interview routine on documentary shoots was the same: put up a COB light, add a softbox, a grid, and a diffusion layer, and lose at least five minutes before the first question. The OrBrella turns this around. Eight LED strips sit on the ribs of a 58cm / 22.8 in umbrella and fire inward at the white fabric, so the source and the diffusion are one object. It opens in about five seconds, and in our comparison, the total setup takes around 15 seconds, against three to five minutes for a COB with a softbox.

On a face, the result is the wraparound, book-light quality that normally needs a bounce, a frame, and a stand for each. A supplied cap goes over the front if you want it even softer. Stefan Karle, CEO of DoPchoice, mentored me through the prototypes and helped us choose the diffusion fabric.

Two lights in one bag

When you need more punch, you press the knob at the end of a strip, pull it off its USB-C connector, and flip it so it faces forward. Each strip flips individually, so you can run half bounced and half direct. For me, this is the part I am proudest of, because it means one fixture in the bag instead of a soft light plus a harder key.

The OrBrella FM 60B is a 60W bi-color fixture with a range of 2,700 to 6,500K plus green/magenta correction. In my opinion, the green/magenta control matters most on location, where mixed fluorescent and daylight is exactly what a real room gives you. We chose 60W on purpose because we found it sufficient for sit-down indoor interviews.

Small, light, and flexible on power

Folded, the light is 34cm / 13.4in long and weighs 1.3kg / 2.87lb, so it fits in a camera bag next to a body and two lenses. Power runs through a separate control box on a permanently attached cable, so there is no cable to forget. The box takes a V-mount battery, USB-C from a power bank or laptop charger, or mains power. A Sony NP-F plate is available as an accessory. On a 99Wh V-mount battery, you get about 1.5 hours of runtime.

You control intensity, color temperature, and green/magenta on the box itself, or through the SmallRig app with NFC pairing. This way, you can trim the light from your chair while you set up the interview.

One honest reminder: the images you see here show a prototype. The light is still under development, and small details may change before the first batch ships.

Price and availability

Until November 8, 2026, the OrBrella FM 60B is $169.99 / €178.90 on SmallRig’s campaign page. Right after the campaign closes, the price goes up by $80. The reason is simple: the cost of components has gone up since we first set the retail price. The first batch is expected to ship on January 20, 2027. For more information, please visit our crowdfunding campaign here.

Before I close, a big thank you to the SmallRig team, to Stefan Karle (DoPchoice) for his patience and guidance, and to everyone who has already backed the light or stopped by the booth with feedback.

Will you find our light a place in your kit? Please share your thoughts with us in the comment section below!

entry.summary: Barcelona-based startup OFFBIT has announced the M1, a small e-paper display for the camera department that replaces the paper lens chart on the camera body. It also holds the crew list, notes and a gallery of custom images, and everything is set up in a free iOS app. The first b
entry.content:
Barcelona-based startup OFFBIT has announced the M1, a small e-paper display for the camera department that replaces the paper lens chart on the camera body. It also holds the crew list, notes and a gallery of custom images, and everything is set up in a free iOS app. The first batch is limited to 100 units, and pre-orders open on November 11. Let’s take a look at what it offers.

Most camera departments still tape a printed lens chart to the camera or keep it in the AC’s pouch, next to a folded crew list and handwritten notes. The OFFBIT M1 puts that information on one small screen that mounts on the camera body or beside a monitor. OFFBIT founder Bernat Eguiluz, a working cinematographer, started the company in Barcelona in October 2025, and the M1 is its first product. According to OFFBIT, the M1 began as a prototype and was refined on productions with the help of focus pullers and 2nd ACs. Camera assistants are the main users.

E-paper is not new to filmmaking gear; we saw an E-Ink status screen on the Insta360 Mic Pro earlier this year. The M1 is, however, a dedicated reference display with no camera or recording function. It shows lens data, the crew list and notes, and the content comes from a free iPhone app over Bluetooth.

Three pages: lens, crew and notes

Three buttons along the top edge switch between the LENS, CREW and NOTES pages. OFFBIT’s press images show the LENS page as a grid of focal lengths, each with its T-stop and close-focus distance, plus the name of the lens set at the bottom. The CREW page lists names, roles and departments, and according to the OFFBIT website, the app can scan a call sheet to fill it in. NOTES is a free-form page for shot lists, radio channels or equipment lists, and the app can also scan a shooting plan into it.

A long press on the center button opens the patch gallery. It holds up to 25 custom images, such as production logos or crew photos. The app converts any image from the phone gallery to a bitmap and sends it to the M1, where the user switches between patches on the device itself. A fourth button on the left side handles pairing and settings.

Screen, housing and battery

The M1 has a 3.1-inch, 320 x 240 pixel black-and-white e-paper screen behind matte Gorilla Glass with an anti-reflective finish. According to the company, it stays readable in direct sunlight. The housing is CNC-machined from 6061 aluminum with a black anodized finish, and the device measures 85 x 60 x 10mm (3.35 x 2.36 x 0.39in) and weighs 71g (2.5oz). OFFBIT rates the 450mAh battery at up to three weeks on a single charge, and the M1 charges via USB-C. It connects to the phone over Bluetooth 5.0 LE.

Set up in the app, not on the device

All content is prepared in the free OFFBIT app and sent to the M1 over Bluetooth. The app includes a database of more than 2,500 lenses and supports custom lenses, which are stored locally. It does not need an account, and it works offline. According to OFFBIT, a connection is necessary only for app and firmware updates, and firmware updates are wireless and free. The company says a project takes minutes to build, and after that the device stays on the camera until something changes.

At launch, the app is available only for iOS on the App Store. An Android version is in development, but OFFBIT gives no release date. OFFBIT also states on its website that it does not sell user data and that there is no subscription.

Mounting and the M1 Backplate

The M1 has a flat back and attaches with Velcro. The box contains the device, eight Velcro loop strips and a welcome card. OFFBIT does not include a USB-C cable, and the website lists the charging input as 5V / 1A.

For camera bodies without a flat surface, OFFBIT offers the M1 Backplate (M1-BP) for €35. It is an aluminum plate with two 1/4″-20 threads and a locking 3/8″-16 point. The M1 attaches to the plate with Velcro, and the plate then mounts to a cage, a magic arm or a monitor.

“M1 saves prep time, but the real difference is on set: lenses, crew, notes and the shooting plan, all in one place. You stop looking for the paper that went missing,” says Bernat.

Current limitations

The M1 is a first product from a new company, and the first batch is small. The app is iOS only, so crews on Android phones cannot use the M1 yet. The screen is black and white at 320 x 240 pixels, which suits text and simple graphics, and patches are converted to a bitmap image. The three-week battery figure is a manufacturer claim. Shipping is limited to Spain and the rest of the EU at first, and the UK, the US and other markets are planned for spring 2027. OFFBIT has not announced US dollar or British pound prices.

Price and availability

The OFFBIT M1 costs €199 including VAT, and the M1 Backplate costs €35. Batch 01 is limited to 100 units, with a maximum of three per person. Pre-orders open on November 11, 2026, at 11:11 CET on the OFFBIT website, with full payment at checkout. Batch 01 ships to Spain and the rest of the EU in December 2026. At the time of writing, B&H and CVP do not list the M1. For more information, visit OFFBIT’s press page.

Would a small e-paper display replace the paper lens chart on your camera, or does tape and paper still do the job? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!
